prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse floor-plane layout: the bottom edge and the camera wearer’s partly visible torso/feet are nearest (roughly 0–0.5 m), nearby people entering along the lower edges are about 0.5–1.5 m away, and people near the top are several metres away (roughly 3–6 m). Across the five frames, the nearby figures shift laterally through the wearer’s field of view while the more distant figures remain toward the upper edge; overlapping bright silhouettes indicate partial occlusion close to the camera. It makes near-versus-far ordering and the distance gradient across the floor clearer than RGB alone, but provides little reliable information about facing direction or gaze. The metric distances are only rough because the map has no scale, washes out nearby regions to white, merges some people with the foreground, and contains soft or incomplete boundaries around legs and partly out-of-view bodies.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates multiple people from the floor and identifies a skateboard in the leftmost frame, making object identity and overlap clearer than in RGB; most people are only partly visible, with several clipped by the top, bottom, left, or right borders. Their masks show relative placement but not dependable metric range: lower masks correspond roughly to people within about 0.5–2 m of the wearer, while upper masks are likely around 3–6 m away, and separated masks at similar heights are roughly 1–3 m apart laterally. Across the sequence, person instances move from left to right or enter and leave the edges, while the skateboard is visible only at the far left; some lower people overlap or nearly overlap in image space, indicating occlusion. Facing direction and gaze cannot be established reliably from these masks, and arm’s reach can only be inferred for figures touching the lower edge; the map is unreliable where bodies are fragmented, mislabeled as separate instances, reduced to tiny patches, or confused with the skateboard.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it provides no detected body or hand skeletons and supports no spatial estimates of joint position, facing direction, gaze, reach, or interpersonal distance. It therefore adds nothing beyond the RGB for scene layout, occlusion, or motion across time. The missing detections are unreliable because several people and limbs are plainly visible in the RGB and segmentation strips, including figures near the camera and others farther ahead. No approach, retreat, turning, or arm’s-reach relationship can be inferred from this map itself.
